column2: Fit the S3 onto the expansion board: the USB-C port faces the USB symbol (number 7). Match the S3's 3V3 pin with the board's 3V3 row.
Plug the USB-C cable into the S3 port labeled COM or UART. If the label is unreadable, try one, then the other in step 4 if no text appears.
Set up the Arduino IDE as in the table below, then choose the port that appears.
Upload the test code. Serial Monitor at 115200.
Measure the 3V3 block (number 2) to GND: it must be about 3.3 V.
Unplug the USB. Install the LovyanGFX library (lovyan03) from the Library Manager.
Three columns become the SPI bus: wires from the S pin IO12 → a2, IO11 → a5, IO13 → a8.

Connect the display pins according to the diagram. Read the pin names on the back of the display: on your module the order from the bottom is VCC, GND, CS, RESET, DC, SDI(MOSI), SCK, LED, SDO(MISO), T_CLK, T_CS, T_DIN, T_DO, T_IRQ. One breadboard column has 5 holes (a-e), so the display's SCK goes to b2, T_CLK to c2, and so on.

The display's SDO(MISO) is left unconnected. On many of these red modules, the display's SDO pin does not "stay quiet" when the display is not in use, which disrupts touch and the SD card. The display does not need to be read.
The slot on the back of your display is full-size SD, not micro SD, so your SanDisk 32 GB goes straight in without an adapter. Slide the small lock on the left side of the card up (not LOCK).
On the laptop, check the card format: a 32 GB card is usually already FAT32. If it says exFAT or NTFS, reformat as FAT32 (the card's contents are erased, move them off first).
Copy one or two MP3 songs to the main folder, with short names and no spaces (for example lagu1.mp3).
On the right edge of your display are 4 empty holes labeled (from the top) SD_SCK, SD_MISO, SD_MOSI, SD_CS. Solder 4 pin headers there.
Connect: SD_SCK → column 2 (d2), SD_MOSI → column 5 (d5), SD_MISO → column 8 (d8), SD_CS → the S pin IO21.
Insert the SD card into the slot on the back of the display until it clicks, the gold contacts facing the board. Upload the test code.
Your MAX98357A already has pin headers and a screw terminal, so no soldering is needed. The pin names are printed on the front (LRC, BCLK, DIN, GAIN, SD, GND, Vin).

First check the ohms of your boxed speaker: look at the sticker on the back, or measure its two wires with a multimeter on the 200 Ω scale. About 3-4 Ω means a 4 Ω speaker, about 6-8 Ω means 8 Ω. Both are safe for the MAX98357A (4-8 Ω).

The white connector on the speaker wire ends does not fit the terminal. Cut the connector off, strip 5 mm from each wire, twist the strands, then clamp them in the terminal: red to ⊕, black to ⊖. Tighten the screws then tug gently to check.
Vin → the red line (3.3 V, for the table), GND → the blue line.
BCLK → S IO4, LRC → S IO5, DIN → S IO7. GAIN and SD are left empty.
Upload the test code (no extra library).
Solder the pin header to the INMP441 if it is not there yet. The round part with the small hole is the sound hole; do not cover it.
VDD → the red line (3.3 V; the INMP441 must not get 5 V), GND and L/R → the blue line.
Upload the test code, open Tools → Serial Plotter. Stay quiet, then clap near the microphone.
Unplug the USB from both boards.
S3 IO17 (S) → DevKit row D16 / RX2 (S). S3 IO18 (S) → DevKit row D17 / TX2 (S).
The S3 board's G pin → the 30P board's G pin. Without this GND wire, the UART data is not read.
Plug the USB into the S3 and the DevKit (to the same laptop is fine, two ports). Upload the test code to the S3.
In the S3 Serial Monitor (line ending: Newline) type PING then Q.
With the wheels lifted and the battery switch ON, type M 120 120 800.

Set up breadboard 2 (the second 400-hole breadboard; the first is used by the body). The breadboard has no power of its own: it is powered from the S3 expansion board. One wire from the 3V3 pin in the 3V3 block of the S3 expansion board → the top red line, one wire from the G pin of the S3 expansion board → the top blue line. The display, MAX98357A, and INMP441 get power from these two lines (the S3 itself runs on USB in desk mode). The MAX98357A and INMP441 are later plugged into this breadboard, from column 12 upward.

Plug in the USB, open the Serial Monitor (115200) first, then upload the test code. The test runs by itself in 5 steps and writes in the Serial Monitor what you need to do, and what is wrong if something fails.

Step 1, colors: the screen turns red, green, blue, white, black, with the color name written in the middle. Each color must fill the whole screen and match its name. If red and blue are swapped, just continue: it is fixed in step 2.

Step 2, orientation: hold the screen landscape, the way you will see it on the robot. The screen shows a white border, the words KIRI ATAS to KANAN BAWAH (top left to bottom right) in the four corners, and a green arrow pointing up. Type a number 0 to 7 and Enter in the Serial Monitor until the text reads normally (not mirrored), the border is complete, and KIRI ATAS is at the top left. At the top there are three boxes MERAH, HIJAU, BIRU (red, green, blue): if red and blue are swapped, type w and Enter. When everything is right, type y and Enter. Your red module turned out to be a native landscape 320 x 240 panel with RGB color order and orientation 6, so the test uses those settings from the start; usually typing y is enough. Orientation 4 is the same as 6 but turned half a circle, for a screen mounted upside down. If with every number part of the screen is not cleared or the border is cut off, type g and Enter to switch the panel type, then try the numbers again.
Step 3, touch wiring: do not touch the screen for 2 seconds, then press the middle of the screen when asked. The test checks the T_ wires itself and tells you which wire to check if it fails.

Step 4, calibration: press exactly the center of each + mark with a stylus or fingernail, hold for 1 second, lift. There are 5 marks, then 1 test mark. The test calculates how far off it is, and repeats the calibration if it is more than 15 pixels.

Step 5, drawing: draw on the screen and tap the 5 gray circles. The orientation and calibration are saved automatically in the S3 memory and used by the SD test and the robot code, so the orientation number does not need to be typed into other code.
